title: Gemini North Back On Sky With Dazzling Image of Supernova in the Pinwheel Galaxy
caption: Supernova SN 2023ixf in the Pinwheel Galaxy, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
celestial: M101, Pinwheel Galaxy, SN 2023ixf · constellation Ursa Major · about 23 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Image Processing: J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Rodriguez (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab), T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab). · Astronomical processing done with DRAGONS 3.1.

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A bright point of light at lower left sits on a spiral arm of the Pinwheel Galaxy, Messier 101. That point is SN 2023ixf, an exploding star, and this image was the first observation Gemini North made after its primary mirror was repaired and refurbished.

The supernova was discovered on 19 May by the Japanese astronomer Koichi Itagaki, and it is described as the nearest supernova spotted in the past five years. The Pinwheel Galaxy lies about 23 million light-years away in Ursa Major.

A supernova is the explosion of a star, which can for a while outshine huge numbers of ordinary stars before fading over the following weeks and months. Because it changes so quickly, astronomers try to observe a new one early and follow it as it evolves. For Gemini North, which belongs to the International Gemini Observatory run by NSF NOIRLab, it made a fitting target for a return to observing.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (10.12 x 5.36 arcminutes) and distance (23 million light years), the frame spans roughly 68,000 × 36,000 light-years. Its light set out about 23 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini North through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The long exposure brings out the galaxy's faint spiral arms far more clearly than the eye could through a telescope.
